analysis.one_liner: Replaces direct farm subsidy checks with price-loss payments, expands subsidized crop insurance, and tightens SNAP eligibility rules.
analysis.headline: The House Agriculture Committee approved the five-year farm bill 35–11, but the bill was never brought to the House floor for a vote and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the House's five-year rewrite of the farm bill. It would have ended the old system of automatic yearly checks to farmers ("direct payments") and replaced it with payments triggered when crop prices or revenues fall, alongside expanded federally subsidized crop insurance, a new dairy margin program, and continued sugar loans. It would have kept food stamps (SNAP) and dozens of farm, conservation, rural development, and research programs running through fiscal 2017 — while tightening SNAP eligibility, blocking a Clean Water Act permit requirement for pesticide spraying over waterways, and repealing some livestock-market regulations.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of the major program crops (corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, rice, peanuts, sugar) would continue receiving federal support through price-loss and revenue-loss payments, marketing loans, and expanded crop insurance. Crop insurance companies would gain a permanently enlarged, federally subsidized market. Dairy producers would get a new margin protection program, and sugar processors would keep nonrecourse federal loans. SNAP participants would see the program extended through fiscal 2017.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commodity farmers, crop insurers, sugar and dairy producers

how_it_helps.text: It repeals direct payments — fixed checks paid to farmers regardless of prices or whether they farm — after the 2012 crop year, replacing them with price loss coverage or county revenue loss coverage for crop years 2013 through 2017.

It expands crop insurance, adding a supplemental coverage option with the federal government covering 70% of premiums, making the enterprise-unit premium subsidy permanent, and creating new income-protection plans for upland cotton and peanut producers.

It extends SNAP, the largest federal food assistance program, through fiscal year 2017, along with food distribution on Indian reservations, emergency food purchases, and senior farmers' market nutrition benefits.

It extends dozens of conservation, rural development, credit, research, forestry, and energy programs through fiscal 2017, including disaster assistance for livestock losses from drought, fire, and disease.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the commodity payments, expanded crop insurance subsidies, sugar loans, and dairy margin program. SNAP recipients who fell under the revised eligibility rules would lose benefits. Water quality and livestock producers would bear the cost of rolled-back environmental and market rules, and states would be preempted from setting stricter standards on agricultural products sold across state lines.

drawbacks.text: The bill tightens SNAP eligibility rules — ending benefits for lottery and gambling winners, excluding medical marijuana expenses from deductions, and revising participant eligibility and disqualifications — which critics said would cut food aid to low-income households.

It includes the Reducing Regulatory Burdens Act, which prohibits the EPA or states from requiring Clean Water Act permits for pesticide discharges into navigable waters, removing a water-quality protection.
It repeals regulations issued under the Packers and Stockyards Act, rolling back rules that governed fair practices in livestock markets between producers and meatpackers.
It sets the adjusted gross income cap for receiving farm program benefits at $950,000, meaning large and well-off farming operations would remain eligible for payments.
It prohibits state and local governments from imposing standards on agricultural products produced in other states beyond federal law, overriding stricter state rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reform of direct payments is real but incomplete: the money is redirected into price-loss payments and larger crop insurance subsidies that would still flow disproportionately to larger growers, and the income cap of $950,000 leaves substantial subsidies for wealthy operations. The nutrition title keeps SNAP running, which matters to tens of millions of households, but the bill pairs that with eligibility restrictions, a pesticide-discharge permitting rollback, and repealed livestock-market rules. On balance the bill serves organized agricultural interests more than taxpayers, though its death also meant the nutrition cuts never took effect.

outcome.mechanism: The Agriculture Committee approved it 35–11 and it sat on the House calendar awaiting floor scheduling, but House leaders never called it up, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Lucas introduced the bill on July 9, 2012, for himself and Representative Collin Peterson, the committee's top Democrat.
The House Agriculture Committee marked the bill up on July 11 and ordered it reported by a vote of 35 to 11; it was formally reported with amendments on September 13, 2012, as H. Rept. 112-669.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting floor scheduling — but no floor vote ever occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

Because the bill never became law, the SNAP eligibility changes, pesticide permitting rollback, and Packers and Stockyards repeals it contained never took effect, and existing farm programs continued under prior law until a successor bill passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income households came out ahead in the near term because the bill's SNAP eligibility cuts never became law. Large commodity producers also came out ahead, since existing farm programs — including the direct payments this bill would have repealed — continued unchanged until a successor farm bill was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food-stamp recipients and incumbent farm programs

for.what_they_did: Joined Lucas in introducing the bill and was its sole cosponsor.

against.name: John Boehner

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a Republican chairman and the committee's top Democrat and was reported 35–11, but it never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call party split exists; the record does not show the party breakdown of the 11 no votes in committee.

industries.note: The bill repeals direct payments but steers producers toward federally subsidized crop insurance, adding a supplemental coverage option with the government covering 70% of premiums and making enterprise-unit subsidies permanent. Private insurers sell these policies and are reimbursed for administrative costs, locking in their role as the federal government's risk-management channel at taxpayer expense.

industries.industry: Commodity crop producers (corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, rice, peanuts)
industries.note: The bill replaces direct checks with price-loss and revenue-loss payments, marketing loans, and new cotton and peanut insurance plans, keeping federal support flowing to program-crop farms. Payments are tied to base acres and yields, so benefits concentrate in the largest operations while taxpayers cover the cost.

The bill continues the sugar program of federal nonrecourse loans through crop year 2017 and suspends permanent price-support authority only through 2017, keeping the supply-control system intact. The sugar program holds domestic sugar prices above world levels, which raises costs for food consumers.

The bill replaces dairy price supports with a margin protection program that pays producers when feed-cost-adjusted margins fall thin, plus a stabilization program to curb supply. Taxpayers fund the payments, and supply management can raise retail milk prices.

The bill's Reducing Regulatory Burdens Act bars the EPA and states from requiring Clean Water Act permits for pesticide discharges into navigable waters. This removes a water-quality safeguard, shifting pollution risk to the public.

The bill repeals regulations issued under the Packers and Stockyards Act, easing oversight of packer conduct in livestock markets. Livestock producers lose protections against unfair practices in those markets.
